sections.title: Page 3

summary.text: The introductory page and first part of the contents of the 1986 LAV/HTLV-III guidelines, explaining that they are broad, based on Member State experience and WHO collaborating centres, and still partly under development. The contents list sections on the virus, transmission, clinical features, laboratory detection, case definitions and precautions for various health and non-health workers.

sections.extract: GUIDELINES FOR THE PREVENTION AND CONTROL OF INFECTION WITH LAV/HTLV-IIY WHO has committed itself to the preparation and distribution of guidelines for the prevention and control of infection with LAV/HTLV-III. are broad in nature and therefore suitable for international application. They are based on the experience of many member countries and advice from the WHO AIDS and Biosafety Collaborating Centres. The

summary.text: Continues the contents of the 1986 LAV/HTLV-III guidelines, listing planned sections on guidance for health professionals, high-risk groups and the general population, and disinfection and sterilization.

sections.title: Page 5

summary.text: Introduces the guidelines as part of the WHO AIDS Control Programme, aimed at public health authorities and health professionals who must adapt them to local settings, and notes they will be revised as knowledge grows. It describes the virus and states that only blood and semen have been implicated in transmission, through sexual, parenteral and perinatal routes.

sections.extract: WHO/CDS/ATDS/86.1 page 3 GUIDELINES FOR THE PREVENTION AND CONTROL OF INFECTION WITH LAV/HTLV-II1 1. Introduction -An important component of the WHO AIDS Control Programme (ACP) is preparation and distribution of guidelines, manuals and educational materials on prevention and control of LAV/HTLV-III infections for professional personnel, for groups at risk and for the general public. The ultimate goal of the ACP

sections.title: Page 6

summary.text: Explains that sexual transmission is the most important route worldwide, alongside transmission through blood, blood products, shared needles and from mother to child, and that the virus is not spread by casual contact, insects, food or water. It begins describing clinical features and laboratory methods for detecting infection.

sections.extract: WHO/CDS/AIDS/86.1 page 4 Worldwide, the most important wode of transmission is sexual, LAV/RTLV-ILL can spread bi-directionally between heterosexual or homosexual partners, Transmission of LAV/ATLV-III through semen donation has also been documented, Parenteral LAV/HTLV-IIL transmission can occur through transfusion of whole blood, blood cells, platelets, or factors VIII or IX derived from contaminated human plasma,

sections.title: Page 7

summary.text: Describes antibody testing by ELISA, which is highly sensitive but gives some false positives, so repeatedly reactive samples should be confirmed with another test. It then introduces the WHO/CDC case definition of AIDS based on opportunistic diseases indicating cellular immunodeficiency.

sections.extract: WHO/CDS/AIDS/86.1 page 5 infection in the community, assessing the likelihood that an individual has been exposed to LAV/HILV-III, and evaluating various methods of preventing or treating the disease, At present, the only practical approach for routine or large-scale testing is detection of antibody to LAV/HTLV-III and the enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) is the antibody detection method most frequently

sections.title: Page 8

summary.text: Completes the WHO/CDC AIDS case definition, including exclusion criteria based on negative tests and normal T-helper counts. It then gives the clinical case definitions for adults and begins the definition for paediatric AIDS.

sections.title: Page 9

summary.text: Lists major and minor signs for the clinical definition of paediatric AIDS and calls for evaluating clinical definitions in different settings. It opens the recommendations for health care workers, stressing avoidance of exposure to patients' blood and keeping workers with weeping lesions from direct patient contact.

sections.title: Page 10

summary.text: Sets out precautions for health care workers against bloodborne infections, including careful handling and disposal of sharps without recapping, safe destruction of disposable needles and syringes, and use of gloves, gowns and masks where appropriate. It also covers handling of specimens, waste and reusable instruments, including those with lenses.

sections.extract: WHO/CDS/ATDS /86.1 page & requires tigorous sterilization of reusable equipment such as needles, syringes and skin~plercing instruments. 2.1 Precautions for HCWs These precautions represent prudent practices that apply to preventing transmission of all bloodborne infections and should be used routinely. 2.4.1. Sharp items (needles, scalpel blades, and other instruments) should be considered as potentially infective,

sections.title: Page 11

summary.text: Recommends disposable or safely sterilized needles and syringes, explains that single-room isolation is not usually needed except in specific circumstances, and advises on resuscitation equipment. It also covers precautions for home care and pre-hospital emergency care providers.

sections.extract: WHO/CDS/ATDS/86.1 page 9 2.1.6, Disposable needles and syringes are preferred. Only needle-locking syringes or one-piece needle-syringe units should be used to aspirate fluids from patients, so that collected fluid can be safely discharged through the needle, if desired, If reusable syringes are employed, they must be sterilized before reuse (see section 7.3) and special care must be taken in handling to avoid

sections.title: Page 12

summary.text: Describes managing needlestick or mucous membrane exposures, including assessing the source patient and testing and following up exposed workers for up to a year. It then sets out laboratory precautions, such as using biological safety cabinets for procedures likely to create aerosols.

sections.extract: WHO/CDS/AIDS/86,1 page 10 blood or other body fluids should be used once and disposed or be thoroughly cleaned and disinfected (see section 7,1). 2.4 Management of parenteral and mucous membrane exposure lt a HCW has a parenteral (e.g,, needlestick or cut) or mucous membrane (e.g., splash to eye or mouth) exposure to blood or other body fluids, the source patient should be assessed clinically and epidemiologically

sections.title: Page 13

summary.text: Continues laboratory precautions, including shielding cell sorters, decontaminating surfaces and materials, hand washing and banning eating or smoking in the laboratory, and gives precautions for animal work. Sections on dental care, necropsies and morticians are marked as still in preparation.

sections.extract: WHO/CDS/ATDS/86.1 page 11 eges. Fluorescent activated cell sorters generate droplets that could potentially result in infectious aerosols, Translucent plastic shielding between the droplet-collecting area and the equipment operator should be used to reduce the presently uncertain magnitude of this risk, Primary containment devices are also used in handling materials that might contain concentrated infectious agents

sections.title: Page 14

summary.text: Covers non-health care workers, advising that personal service workers who pierce the skin follow health worker precautions and properly disinfect instruments, though no transmission has been documented in such settings. It states that food service workers with LAV/HTLV-III need not be restricted from work unless they have other illnesses.

sections.extract: WHO/CDS/AIDS/86,1 page 12 2.9 Eye examiners* 3. Considerations relevant to non health cate workers 3.1 Personal service workers Personal service workers are defined as individuals whose occupations involve close personal contact with clients (e.g. hairdressers, barbers, manicurists, pedicurists, massage therapists). Personal service workers whose services (tattoolng, ear piercing, acupuncture, etc.) require needles

sections.title: Page 15

summary.text: States that infected workers in offices, schools and other settings pose no known risk and should not be restricted, with routine cleaning of contaminated equipment. It notes some sections are pending and begins the section on disinfection, describing sodium hypochlorite and differences in strength of household bleach products between countries.

sections.extract: wHo/cps/AIDS/86.1 page 13 3,3 Workers sharing same work environment No known risk of transmission to coworkers, clients of consumers exists from LAV/HTLV-III infected workers in other settings (e.g. offices, schools, factories, construction sites), Workers known to be infected with LAV/HTLV-III should not be restricted from work solely based on this finding. summary.text: Gives contact times for disinfectants such as formalin, ethanol and glutaraldehyde, and describes sterilization by autoclaving or boiling and high-level disinfection of heat-sensitive equipment. It sets out a step-by-step method for processing reusable needles and syringes.

sections.title: Page 19

summary.text: Presents the first page of WHO's provisional 1986 AIDS reporting form, asking countries to report cases meeting the WHO/CDC or clinical definitions and how many clinical cases were serotested and confirmed. It also asks for cases by age, sex and disease category, such as opportunistic infection or Kaposi's sarcoma, with footnotes on reporting periods and totals.
